front: What are the key terms for urban change?
p1: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of people living in towns and cities; urban growth is a rise in a town's population; a megacity has 10 million+ people.
p2: Natural increase happens when birth rate is higher than death rate; rural-urban migration is the main reason LIC and NEE cities grow so fast.
p3: A push factor is a reason to leave a rural area, a pull factor is a reason to move to the city; a slum has poor quality, often illegal housing lacking clean water, sewers or electricity.
s: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of people living in towns and cities; urban growth is a rise in a town's population; a megacity has 10 million+ people.
Natural increase happens when birth rate is higher than death rate; rural-urban migration is the main reason LIC and NEE cities grow so fast.
A push factor is a reason to leave a rural area, a pull factor is a reason to move to the city; a slum has poor quality, often illegal housing lacking clean water, sewers or electricity.

front: Where is Mumbai?
p1: Mumbai is in Asia → India → the state of Maharashtra; it is the state capital, but NOT the capital of India.
p2: Mumbai lies on the west coast of India, not the east; its port handles 70% of maritime trade and 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
p3: Mumbai has a population of over 21 million → India's largest city and a megacity (10 million+ people).
s: Mumbai is in Asia → India → the state of Maharashtra; it is the state capital, but NOT the capital of India.
Mumbai lies on the west coast of India, not the east; its port handles 70% of maritime trade and 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
Mumbai has a population of over 21 million → India's largest city and a megacity (10 million+ people).

front: Why is Mumbai important?
p1: Regional: capital of Maharashtra → generates 40% of the state's income; 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
p2: National: commercial capital of India → 6% of India's GDP; home to the Bombay Stock Exchange, Reserve Bank of India and Tata Group; its port handles 70% of maritime trade.
p3: International: a top ten centre of commerce in the world; Bollywood is the largest film producer in the world; historic importance to Portugal and Britain makes it a melting pot of cultures.
s: Regional: capital of Maharashtra → generates 40% of the state's income; 3 million people commute in from surrounding areas.
National: commercial capital of India → 6% of India's GDP; home to the Bombay Stock Exchange, Reserve Bank of India and Tata Group; its port handles 70% of maritime trade.
International: a top ten centre of commerce in the world; Bollywood is the largest film producer in the world; historic importance to Portugal and Britain makes it a melting pot of cultures.

front: Why is Mumbai growing so rapidly?
p1: Rural-urban migration is the first cause → 480 migrants arrive in Mumbai each day.
p2: Push: average wage in rural Maharashtra is as low as $1 a day; pull: it is $20 a day in Mumbai, though less in the informal sector; many jobs are informal, e.g. hawkers and laundry workers.
p3: Natural increase is the second cause → a high birth rate; it is birth rate minus death rate.
s: Rural-urban migration is the first cause → 480 migrants arrive in Mumbai each day.
Push: average wage in rural Maharashtra is as low as $1 a day; pull: it is $20 a day in Mumbai, though less in the informal sector; many jobs are informal, e.g. hawkers and laundry workers.
Natural increase is the second cause → a high birth rate; it is birth rate minus death rate.

front: What opportunities does Mumbai offer?
p1: Education: primary and secondary schools with free education up to certain ages; University of Mumbai is world renowned; literacy rate 89.7% (slums: 69%+).
p2: Health and resources: healthcare is better than the rest of India; 98% of people have electricity and water supply.
p3: Industry: financial capital of India with the Bombay Stock Exchange and Tata Group; informal sector jobs in recycling, leather tanning and pottery; call centres in Navi Mumbai after government tax breaks and IT parks.
s: Education: primary and secondary schools with free education up to certain ages; University of Mumbai is world renowned; literacy rate 89.7% (slums: 69%+).
Health and resources: healthcare is better than the rest of India; 98% of people have electricity and water supply.

Industry: financial capital of India with the Bombay Stock Exchange and Tata Group; informal sector jobs in recycling, leather tanning and pottery; call centres in Navi Mumbai after government tax breaks and IT parks.

front: What challenges does Dharavi face?
p1: Dharavi is one of the largest slums in Asia, in the heart of Mumbai → overcrowding with about a million people.
p2: 500 people share one public toilet and open sewers run through the streets → water-borne disease such as typhoid and diphtheria.
p3: One third of residents have experienced crime; residents have no legal right to the land → it can be cleared at any time.
s: Dharavi is one of the largest slums in Asia, in the heart of Mumbai → overcrowding with about a million people.
500 people share one public toilet and open sewers run through the streets → water-borne disease such as typhoid and diphtheria.
One third of residents have experienced crime; residents have no legal right to the land → it can be cleared at any time.

front: Why do sanitation and waste cause problems in Dharavi?
p1: Slum areas often lack proper sewage, so dirty water flows into the river; water-borne disease spreads, including cholera where rubbish dumps infect water supplies.
p2: There is no proper city-wide rubbish collection, and none organised in Dharavi, so open dumps attract rats and cockroaches → disease.
p3: Positive: ragpickers collect and recycle plastic → this creates hundreds of thousands of jobs.
s: Slum areas often lack proper sewage, so dirty water flows into the river; water-borne disease spreads, including cholera where rubbish dumps infect water supplies.
There is no proper city-wide rubbish collection, and none organised in Dharavi, so open dumps attract rats and cockroaches → disease.
Positive: ragpickers collect and recycle plastic → this creates hundreds of thousands of jobs.

front: How is informal work both a strength and a problem?
p1: Strength: thousands of small workshops and home businesses in Dharavi do recycling, leather tanning and pottery work for residents.
p2: Problem: informal work has no contracts, no legal protections and little job security; it is not taxed by the government → the city cannot gain taxes.
p3: Problem: it traps many residents in low-income, unstable work → young people leave education early to work.
s: Strength: thousands of small workshops and home businesses in Dharavi do recycling, leather tanning and pottery work for residents.
Problem: informal work has no contracts, no legal protections and little job security; it is not taxed by the government → the city cannot gain taxes.
Problem: it traps many residents in low-income, unstable work → young people leave education early to work.

front: How polluted are Mumbai's water and air?
p1: The Mithi River flows through the city including Dharavi; 93% of its waste comes from homes and 7% from factories.
p2: About 1,500 factories line the river and many release waste straight in → Water Quality Index 'bad to very bad'.
p3: Smog is common and particulate matter is 15x over the safe limit → asthma and other serious health problems; Mumbai is ranked 4th most polluted megacity in the world.
s: The Mithi River flows through the city including Dharavi; 93% of its waste comes from homes and 7% from factories.
About 1,500 factories line the river and many release waste straight in → Water Quality Index 'bad to very bad'.
Smog is common and particulate matter is 15x over the safe limit → asthma and other serious health problems; Mumbai is ranked 4th most polluted megacity in the world.

front: How bad is traffic congestion in Mumbai?
p1: Mumbai has 1.8 million motor vehicles; private vehicles are up by more than half in 8 years and people spend about 1.5 hours a day stuck in traffic.
p2: Trains built for 1,700 passengers often carry three times that number, so overcrowding is severe on the rail network.
p3: Response: nearly 90% use public transport; a new traffic system is run from a control centre in Mumbai police headquarters.
s: Mumbai has 1.8 million motor vehicles; private vehicles are up by more than half in 8 years and people spend about 1.5 hours a day stuck in traffic.
Trains built for 1,700 passengers often carry three times that number, so overcrowding is severe on the rail network.
Response: nearly 90% use public transport; a new traffic system is run from a control centre in Mumbai police headquarters.

front: How does the Dharavi Sector 5 redevelopment change quality of life?
p1: A $2 billion project in Sector 5 of Dharavi → slum housing demolished and replaced by high-rise tower blocks; 72,000 families rehomed.
p2: Improved: proper plumbing and toilets → less water-borne disease, e.g. cholera; new parks and green space; secure windows and doors.
p3: Worsened: most slum dwellers have no legal right to land → homeless; loss of community (some families there 150 years); flats too small (5 to 10 people in 21 m2); unique culture destroyed.
s: A $2 billion project in Sector 5 of Dharavi → slum housing demolished and replaced by high-rise tower blocks; 72,000 families rehomed.
Improved: proper plumbing and toilets → less water-borne disease, e.g. cholera; new parks and green space; secure windows and doors.
Worsened: most slum dwellers have no legal right to land → homeless; loss of community (some families there 150 years); flats too small (5 to 10 people in 21 m2); unique culture destroyed.

front: What are the key terms in ecosystems?
p1: An ecosystem is producers, consumers and decomposers interacting with each other and with non-living parts; a producer is a plant that uses sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make its own food.
p2: A primary consumer feeds on producers (herbivore) and a secondary consumer feeds on primary consumers (carnivore); a decomposer breaks down dead organisms and returns nutrients to the soil.
p3: A food chain shows how each living thing gets its food, starting with plants; a food web is interlocking food chains; biodiversity is the variety of life in an area.
s: An ecosystem is producers, consumers and decomposers interacting with each other and with non-living parts; a producer is a plant that uses sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make its own food.
A primary consumer feeds on producers (herbivore) and a secondary consumer feeds on primary consumers (carnivore); a decomposer breaks down dead organisms and returns nutrients to the soil.
A food chain shows how each living thing gets its food, starting with plants; a food web is interlocking food chains; biodiversity is the variety of life in an area.

front: What is the global pattern of biomes?
p1: A biome is a large area with similar climate, geology and vegetation, found in bands of latitude around the planet.
p2: Tropical rainforest is very hot and wet, on or around the equator; desert is very hot and very dry, around 30 degrees N and S; tropical savannah is hot, dry grassland with scattered shrubs and trees between rainforest and desert.
p3: Tundra is below freezing at night all year, 'land with no trees'; coniferous forest (taiga) is northern evergreen forest; temperate deciduous forest has four distinct seasons.
s: A biome is a large area with similar climate, geology and vegetation, found in bands of latitude around the planet.

Tropical rainforest is very hot and wet, on or around the equator; desert is very hot and very dry, around 30 degrees N and S; tropical savannah is hot, dry grassland with scattered shrubs and trees between rainforest and desert.
Tundra is below freezing at night all year, 'land with no trees'; coniferous forest (taiga) is northern evergreen forest; temperate deciduous forest has four distinct seasons.

front: Why are rainforests on the equator and deserts near 30 degrees?
p1: The equator is heated intensely by differential heating, so it is hotter than the poles → temperature changes with latitude.
p2: At the equator air rises → cools → condenses → heavy convectional rain; this low pressure zone is the ITCZ (inter-tropical convergence zone).
p3: Air spreads north and south, cools and sinks at about 30 degrees N and S → high pressure → almost no rain → deserts; the loop of rising and sinking air is the Hadley cell.
s: The equator is heated intensely by differential heating, so it is hotter than the poles → temperature changes with latitude.
At the equator air rises → cools → condenses → heavy convectional rain; this low pressure zone is the ITCZ (inter-tropical convergence zone).
Air spreads north and south, cools and sinks at about 30 degrees N and S → high pressure → almost no rain → deserts; the loop of rising and sinking air is the Hadley cell.

front: How will climate change affect Epping Forest?
p1: Epping Forest is deciduous woodland, the most common ecosystem in the UK → the trees lose their leaves each year.
p2: The UK is getting wetter summers and milder temperatures → oak mildew, a fungus, weakens oaks (Oak Decline); warmer winters let insects survive all year → pest populations rise, e.g. Horse Chestnut Leaf Miner.
p3: Windthrow: more wind and wet soils → trees uprooted; the cause is the burning of fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide.
s: Epping Forest is deciduous woodland, the most common ecosystem in the UK → the trees lose their leaves each year.

The UK is getting wetter summers and milder temperatures → oak mildew, a fungus, weakens oaks (Oak Decline); warmer winters let insects survive all year → pest populations rise, e.g. Horse Chestnut Leaf Miner.
Windthrow: more wind and wet soils → trees uprooted; the cause is the burning of fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide.

front: What is a tropical rainforest like?
p1: Found on or around the equator; the Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, spanning 9 countries in South America with 60% in Brazil.
p2: Climate: hot and wet all year with a very small temperature range; rain falls in every month.
p3: Structure: four layers, with emergent trees 40 to 60 m tall; biodiversity is very high, with 6% of the Earth but around 50% of known species.
s: Found on or around the equator; the Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, spanning 9 countries in South America with 60% in Brazil.
Climate: hot and wet all year with a very small temperature range; rain falls in every month.
Structure: four layers, with emergent trees 40 to 60 m tall; biodiversity is very high, with 6% of the Earth but around 50% of known species.

front: Why is the rainforest climate hot and wet?
p1: The sun is overhead at the equator → energy is concentrated on a small surface area; the wettest month is March, with about 314 mm.
p2: Evaporation is rapid, so warm moist air rises → low pressure.
p3: Rising air cools → condensation → clouds → heavy convectional rain, usually in the afternoon; the equator has rising air in the Hadley cell, the ITCZ.
s: The sun is overhead at the equator → energy is concentrated on a small surface area; the wettest month is March, with about 314 mm.
Evaporation is rapid, so warm moist air rises → low pressure.
Rising air cools → condensation → clouds → heavy convectional rain, usually in the afternoon; the equator has rising air in the Hadley cell, the ITCZ.

front: How are rainforest plants adapted?
p1: Emergent trees are very tall (40 to 60 m) → reach the strongest sunlight above the canopy; buttress roots act as an anchor → support tall emergent trees.
p2: Drip tips are pointed leaf ends → heavy rain runs off quickly so leaves are not damaged; glossy, pointed-tip leaves in the canopy repel water.
p3: Canopy plants encase seeds in fruit → animals eat it and spread seeds; emergent trees have lightweight seeds spread by wind; understorey plants have larger leaves for dim light.
s: Emergent trees are very tall (40 to 60 m) → reach the strongest sunlight above the canopy; buttress roots act as an anchor → support tall emergent trees.
Drip tips are pointed leaf ends → heavy rain runs off quickly so leaves are not damaged; glossy, pointed-tip leaves in the canopy repel water.
Canopy plants encase seeds in fruit → animals eat it and spread seeds; emergent trees have lightweight seeds spread by wind; understorey plants have larger leaves for dim light.

front: How are rainforest animals adapted?
p1: Emergent layer animals fly or glide, e.g. birds, bats, gliders and butterflies.
p2: Most animals live in the canopy because there is plenty of fruit; the Boto (pink river dolphin) lives in Amazon freshwater habitats.
p3: Decomposers such as termites, slugs, worms and fungi live on the forest floor.
s: Emergent layer animals fly or glide, e.g. birds, bats, gliders and butterflies.
Most animals live in the canopy because there is plenty of fruit; the Boto (pink river dolphin) lives in Amazon freshwater habitats.
Decomposers such as termites, slugs, worms and fungi live on the forest floor.

front: Why is rainforest soil nutrient-rich but fragile?
p1: The soil is nutrient-rich but shallow, and the trees shed their leaves all year.
p2: Dead leaves break down rapidly on the warm damp floor with insects, forming humus that roots absorb quickly → nutrients are used up quickly.
p3: After clearance there is no canopy → heavy rain washes nutrients out and topsoil into rivers → the soil quickly becomes infertile and cleared land is often abandoned.
s: The soil is nutrient-rich but shallow, and the trees shed their leaves all year.
Dead leaves break down rapidly on the warm damp floor with insects, forming humus that roots absorb quickly → nutrients are used up quickly.
After clearance there is no canopy → heavy rain washes nutrients out and topsoil into rivers → the soil quickly becomes infertile and cleared land is often abandoned.

front: What causes deforestation in the Amazon?
p1: Causes: cattle ranching, commercial farming, subsistence farming, logging, mining, roads, settlement and energy (dams).
p2: Commercial: around 80% of cleared land becomes cattle pasture, with plantations of soya, palm oil and bananas; Brazil is one of the world's largest exporters.
p3: Subsistence: Amerindians have used slash and burn for generations → trees cut and burned for temporary nutrient-rich soil; government gave small amounts of land to some of Brazil's 25 million people.
s: Causes: cattle ranching, commercial farming, subsistence farming, logging, mining, roads, settlement and energy (dams).
Commercial: around 80% of cleared land becomes cattle pasture, with plantations of soya, palm oil and bananas; Brazil is one of the world's largest exporters.
Subsistence: Amerindians have used slash and burn for generations → trees cut and burned for temporary nutrient-rich soil; government gave small amounts of land to some of Brazil's 25 million people.

front: How do logging, mining, roads and dams clear the rainforest?
p1: Logging takes hardwoods such as mahogany for furniture; mining takes iron ore, bauxite and gold, with about 50,000 hectares cleared for gold alone (70,000 football pitches).
p2: Over 12,000 km of new roads have been built, including the Trans-Amazonian Highway (5,300 km) → opens remote areas.
p3: Brazil's population has more than doubled since 1972 and Parauapebas is fast-growing; 74 dams are on Amazon rivers, including Belo Monte (2019).
s: Logging takes hardwoods such as mahogany for furniture; mining takes iron ore, bauxite and gold, with about 50,000 hectares cleared for gold alone (70,000 football pitches).
Over 12,000 km of new roads have been built, including the Trans-Amazonian Highway (5,300 km) → opens remote areas.
Brazil's population has more than doubled since 1972 and Parauapebas is fast-growing; 74 dams are on Amazon rivers, including Belo Monte (2019).

front: What are the impacts of deforestation?
p1: Loss of biodiversity: 137 species lost a day; loss of indigenous people: about 6 million Amerindians in 1500, roughly 200,000 now.
p2: Without a canopy and roots, topsoil is washed away → soil erosion; nutrients are leached within a few years → infertile soil and abandoned land.
p3: Less evapotranspiration from fewer trees → less rainfall, so parts of the forest risk turning to savanna; burning trees releases carbon (the Amazon holds around 100 billion tonnes) → faster global warming.
s: Loss of biodiversity: 137 species lost a day; loss of indigenous people: about 6 million Amerindians in 1500, roughly 200,000 now.
Without a canopy and roots, topsoil is washed away → soil erosion; nutrients are leached within a few years → infertile soil and abandoned land.

Less evapotranspiration from fewer trees → less rainfall, so parts of the forest risk turning to savanna; burning trees releases carbon (the Amazon holds around 100 billion tonnes) → faster global warming.

front: Why are tropical rainforests valuable?
p1: Environment: the forest stores carbon and drives its own water cycle through evapotranspiration; it covers 6% of the Earth but holds around 50% of known species.
p2: Medicines: about 25% of modern medicines come from rainforest plants; the rosy periwinkle treats childhood leukaemia.
p3: People: timber, minerals, farmland, energy and jobs for Brazil; the forest is home to Amerindian groups such as the Kayapo (food, shelter, medicine).
s: Environment: the forest stores carbon and drives its own water cycle through evapotranspiration; it covers 6% of the Earth but holds around 50% of known species.
Medicines: about 25% of modern medicines come from rainforest plants; the rosy periwinkle treats childhood leukaemia.
People: timber, minerals, farmland, energy and jobs for Brazil; the forest is home to Amerindian groups such as the Kayapo (food, shelter, medicine).

front: How can the rainforest be managed sustainably?
p1: Sustainable management means meeting today's needs without damaging the resource for future generations.
p2: Local strategies are ecotourism, and selective logging with replanting; national parks work at national scale, e.g. Tumucumaque National Park (2002), around the size of Switzerland.
p3: International strategies are the timber agreement (ITTA) and debt reduction; charities such as WWF run conservation and education.
s: Sustainable management means meeting today's needs without damaging the resource for future generations.
Local strategies are ecotourism, and selective logging with replanting; national parks work at national scale, e.g. Tumucumaque National Park (2002), around the size of Switzerland.
International strategies are the timber agreement (ITTA) and debt reduction; charities such as WWF run conservation and education.

front: What are the pros and cons of local rainforest management?
p1: Ecotourism uses small, locally owned resorts of sustainable materials with local guides → money goes to local people, so the forest is worth more standing than cleared.
p2: Limit: ecotourism reaches only a few thousand people a year in the Amazon.
p3: Selective logging cuts only mature or valuable trees so the forest can recover and loggers still earn; but felled trees damage others, replanting is expensive, and secondary forest takes over 20 years to regain 80% of biodiversity.
s: Ecotourism uses small, locally owned resorts of sustainable materials with local guides → money goes to local people, so the forest is worth more standing than cleared.
Limit: ecotourism reaches only a few thousand people a year in the Amazon.

Selective logging cuts only mature or valuable trees so the forest can recover and loggers still earn; but felled trees damage others, replanting is expensive, and secondary forest takes over 20 years to regain 80% of biodiversity.

front: How do national parks and education help, and what are their limits?
p1: Tumucumaque National Park (2002) is around the size of Switzerland → it is hard to police illegal logging across such an area.
p2: WWF staff visit schools in rainforest areas to teach why the rainforest matters → this changes attitudes in the long term.
p3: Charities rely on donations, results take a long time, and many people cut forest because they are desperately poor.
s: Tumucumaque National Park (2002) is around the size of Switzerland → it is hard to police illegal logging across such an area.
WWF staff visit schools in rainforest areas to teach why the rainforest matters → this changes attitudes in the long term.
Charities rely on donations, results take a long time, and many people cut forest because they are desperately poor.

front: How do international agreements protect the rainforest?
p1: The International Tropical Timber Agreement (ITTA, 2006) marks hardwood with a registration number proving it came from a managed forest → illegal loggers find it harder to sell wood.
p2: Limits: some illegal timber still reaches market; remote areas are hard to monitor; people who rely on illegal logging lose income.
p3: In a debt-for-nature swap an HIC cancels part of the debt of an LIC or NEE and in return it protects part of its forest; but it cannot earn money from those areas and the promise is hard to enforce.
s: The International Tropical Timber Agreement (ITTA, 2006) marks hardwood with a registration number proving it came from a managed forest → illegal loggers find it harder to sell wood.
Limits: some illegal timber still reaches market; remote areas are hard to monitor; people who rely on illegal logging lose income.
In a debt-for-nature swap an HIC cancels part of the debt of an LIC or NEE and in return it protects part of its forest; but it cannot earn money from those areas and the promise is hard to enforce.

front: What are the key terms in resource management?
p1: Resources are physical supplies humans need to survive; energy security means uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price.
p2: An energy mix is the combination of energy sources used to meet a country's total energy demand; water stress is when a place's water demand cannot be met (in deficit).
p3: Sustainable management means meeting needs today without damaging a resource for future generations.
s: Resources are physical supplies humans need to survive; energy security means uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price.
An energy mix is the combination of energy sources used to meet a country's total energy demand; water stress is when a place's water demand cannot be met (in deficit).
Sustainable management means meeting needs today without damaging a resource for future generations.

front: Why do energy security and resources matter?
p1: A regular supply of food, water and energy is essential for health, a good life, good social relations, security and freedom of choice → quality of life and economic well-being improve.
p2: An energy secure country has a reliable and uninterrupted supply, an affordable and competitively priced supply, and an accessible and available supply.
p3: It also has a domestic energy mix that is not reliant on imports; countries can generate their own energy or import it; the booklet links the war in Ukraine to energy security and the cost of living.
s: A regular supply of food, water and energy is essential for health, a good life, good social relations, security and freedom of choice → quality of life and economic well-being improve.
An energy secure country has a reliable and uninterrupted supply, an affordable and competitively priced supply, and an accessible and available supply.
It also has a domestic energy mix that is not reliant on imports; countries can generate their own energy or import it; the booklet links the war in Ukraine to energy security and the cost of living.

front: What factors affect energy supply?
p1: Physical: just 1% of the Sahara would provide enough solar energy for the world; Iceland has hot rocks near the surface on a constructive boundary → geothermal energy.
p2: North Sea gas is mostly extracted → harder and costlier to get more; the USA is energy secure through fracking (shale gas).
p3: Pirates seized an oil tanker off Somalia; Germany is planning to stop nuclear power (waste concerns); the Nembe Creek pipeline in the Niger delta had 53 leaks from suspected oil thieves.
s: Physical: just 1% of the Sahara would provide enough solar energy for the world; Iceland has hot rocks near the surface on a constructive boundary → geothermal energy.
North Sea gas is mostly extracted → harder and costlier to get more; the USA is energy secure through fracking (shale gas).
Pirates seized an oil tanker off Somalia; Germany is planning to stop nuclear power (waste concerns); the Nembe Creek pipeline in the Niger delta had 53 leaks from suspected oil thieves.

front: How have UK food habits changed?
p1: Before the 1950s food was mostly seasonal; from the 1950s agribusiness grew and food costs fell, with environmental and social impacts.
p2: In 1951 the first UK supermarket opened in Streatham → supermarkets gained control of supply chains and drove prices down; globalisation brought strawberries in January and fruit grown in polytunnels in southern Spain, shipped or flown in refrigerated.
p3: From the 1990s some people try to buy locally produced food; recent years show growing demand for organic food; lower greenhouse gas emissions come with lower food miles.
s: Before the 1950s food was mostly seasonal; from the 1950s agribusiness grew and food costs fell, with environmental and social impacts.

In 1951 the first UK supermarket opened in Streatham → supermarkets gained control of supply chains and drove prices down; globalisation brought strawberries in January and fruit grown in polytunnels in southern Spain, shipped or flown in refrigerated.
From the 1990s some people try to buy locally produced food; recent years show growing demand for organic food; lower greenhouse gas emissions come with lower food miles.

front: Where does the UK's water come from?
p1: Surface water comes from rivers, lakes and reservoirs: 474 sources in England and Wales and 339 in Scotland.
p2: Surface water supplies 64% of England's drinking water and nearly 93% of Wales's.
p3: Groundwater is stored in aquifers (rock, sand and soil): 2,259 sources in England and Wales and 86 in Scotland, but only 30% of England's and 6% of Wales's tap water.
s: Surface water comes from rivers, lakes and reservoirs: 474 sources in England and Wales and 339 in Scotland.
Surface water supplies 64% of England's drinking water and nearly 93% of Wales's.
Groundwater is stored in aquifers (rock, sand and soil): 2,259 sources in England and Wales and 86 in Scotland, but only 30% of England's and 6% of Wales's tap water.

front: Why does a wet country worry about drought?
p1: Some areas of the UK have a water surplus while others have a deficit.
p2: London and 70% of English regions could be under water stress within two decades → severe unless action is taken.
p3: Water transfer schemes move water from surplus areas to deficit areas, e.g. Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland, released into rivers → Newcastle, Sunderland, Durham, Darlington and Middlesbrough.
s: Some areas of the UK have a water surplus while others have a deficit.
London and 70% of English regions could be under water stress within two decades → severe unless action is taken.

Water transfer schemes move water from surplus areas to deficit areas, e.g. Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland, released into rivers → Newcastle, Sunderland, Durham, Darlington and Middlesbrough.

front: Why have water transfer schemes been limited in the UK?
p1: A national water grid (like the electricity grid) has been considered but not developed.
p2: About 5% of UK supply is piped from outside the local area.
p3: Transfer schemes have fallen out of favour because of environmental impact on the donor area, cost and energy use.
s: A national water grid (like the electricity grid) has been considered but not developed.
About 5% of UK supply is piped from outside the local area.
Transfer schemes have fallen out of favour because of environmental impact on the donor area, cost and energy use.

front: What is a hot desert?
p1: A desert is land or climate so dry it supports little vegetation → arid land receives less than 250mm of precipitation a year.
p2: The Sahara covers 9,200,000 km² → it lies 15 to 30° north of the Equator and covers most of northern Africa.
p3: The difference in temperature within one day is the diurnal range; a climate graph shows temperature as a line and precipitation as bars.
s: A desert is land or climate so dry it supports little vegetation → arid land receives less than 250mm of precipitation a year.
The Sahara covers 9,200,000 km² → it lies 15 to 30° north of the Equator and covers most of northern Africa.
The difference in temperature within one day is the diurnal range; a climate graph shows temperature as a line and precipitation as bars.

front: How do plants adapt to hot deserts?
p1: Xerophytes have physical adaptations, e.g. the saguaro cactus → shallow roots 4 to 6 inches deep catch rare rain, the fleshy stem stores water, thin spines replace leaves → less transpiration.
p2: The mesquite tree has tap roots as long as 24 metres → they reach the water table; small, waxy leaves cut water loss and leaves are dropped in droughts.
p3: Ephemerals have behavioural adaptations, e.g. the ocotillo → dormant in dry periods, new leaves after rain, waxy stem coating seals in moisture, up to five cycles a year.
s: Xerophytes have physical adaptations, e.g. the saguaro cactus → shallow roots 4 to 6 inches deep catch rare rain, the fleshy stem stores water, thin spines replace leaves → less transpiration.
The mesquite tree has tap roots as long as 24 metres → they reach the water table; small, waxy leaves cut water loss and leaves are dropped in droughts.
Ephemerals have behavioural adaptations, e.g. the ocotillo → dormant in dry periods, new leaves after rain, waxy stem coating seals in moisture, up to five cycles a year.

front: How do animals adapt to hot deserts?
p1: Fennec fox → large ears dissipate excess body heat, kidneys restrict water loss, sandy colour reflects the Sun's heat, thick fur on the soles protects against hot sand.
p2: Leopard gecko → strictly nocturnal, sleeping by day to limit heat exposure; transparent eyelids protect against sandstorms; solid, crystallised faeces limit water loss.
p3: Gila monster → up to 98% of its life underground in burrows to avoid extreme heat, eating only 5 to 6 times a year; African elephant → huge ears with surface blood vessels cool its blood.
s: Fennec fox → large ears dissipate excess body heat, kidneys restrict water loss, sandy colour reflects the Sun's heat, thick fur on the soles protects against hot sand.
Leopard gecko → strictly nocturnal, sleeping by day to limit heat exposure; transparent eyelids protect against sandstorms; solid, crystallised faeces limit water loss.
Gila monster → up to 98% of its life underground in burrows to avoid extreme heat, eating only 5 to 6 times a year; African elephant → huge ears with surface blood vessels cool its blood.

front: How is energy developed in the Sahara?
p1: Oil was found at Hassi Messaoud in 1956 → now one of North Africa's biggest oilfields, employing 40,000 local people, with Shell and BP.
p2: Challenges → deep in the Sahara, miles from roads, nearest oasis over 40 miles away; overcome by pumping water from aquifers and building a runway.
p3: Noor Ouarzazate in Morocco is a solar complex of about 580 MW → 8,500 construction jobs but only 234 permanent by 2022; mirrors cleaned with piped water.
s: Oil was found at Hassi Messaoud in 1956 → now one of North Africa's biggest oilfields, employing 40,000 local people, with Shell and BP.
Challenges → deep in the Sahara, miles from roads, nearest oasis over 40 miles away; overcome by pumping water from aquifers and building a runway.
Noor Ouarzazate in Morocco is a solar complex of about 580 MW → 8,500 construction jobs but only 234 permanent by 2022; mirrors cleaned with piped water.

front: How do mining and tourism help Morocco?
p1: Morocco is the world's leading exporter of phosphate, holding 75% of global reserves; mining gives about 10% of GDP; it is vital in synthetic fertiliser.
p2: Mining challenges → toxic risks to workers' health and the environment; mining is very water intensive → the company OCP builds desalination plants to supply fresh water.
p3: Tourism employs 2.5 million of Morocco's 35 million people, about 7% of GDP; challenge → only three gateways into the Sahara from Marrakech, each a road journey of several hours.
s: Morocco is the world's leading exporter of phosphate, holding 75% of global reserves; mining gives about 10% of GDP; it is vital in synthetic fertiliser.
Mining challenges → toxic risks to workers' health and the environment; mining is very water intensive → the company OCP builds desalination plants to supply fresh water.
Tourism employs 2.5 million of Morocco's 35 million people, about 7% of GDP; challenge → only three gateways into the Sahara from Marrakech, each a road journey of several hours.

front: What is desertification?
p1: Desertification is the process by which fertile land turns into non-productive desert → it can have natural causes but is also a result of human activity.
p2: The Sahel lies on the fringe of a hot desert → a rainfall index shows whether rainfall is above or below the long-term average.
p3: Deforestation is cutting down trees; erosion is rock or soil worn away and removed by wind, water or ice; infertile soil has no nutrients.
s: Desertification is the process by which fertile land turns into non-productive desert → it can have natural causes but is also a result of human activity.
The Sahel lies on the fringe of a hot desert → a rainfall index shows whether rainfall is above or below the long-term average.
Deforestation is cutting down trees; erosion is rock or soil worn away and removed by wind, water or ice; infertile soil has no nutrients.

front: How can desertification be managed?
p1: Appropriate technology is cheap to make, easy to use and mend, and often takes advantage of local conditions such as a sunny climate.
p2: Afforestation, planting trees, stops soil erosion, holds water and adds nutrients from leaf litter; the African Union's Great Green Wall, launched 2007, is 8,000 km long across 11 countries.
p3: Stone lines 25 to 30 cm high along contours trap rainwater and nutrients; the idea spread from Burkina Faso to Mali and Niger, and it is cheap and quickly learned.
s: Appropriate technology is cheap to make, easy to use and mend, and often takes advantage of local conditions such as a sunny climate.
Afforestation, planting trees, stops soil erosion, holds water and adds nutrients from leaf litter; the African Union's Great Green Wall, launched 2007, is 8,000 km long across 11 countries.
Stone lines 25 to 30 cm high along contours trap rainwater and nutrients; the idea spread from Burkina Faso to Mali and Niger, and it is cheap and quickly learned.

front: Which other strategies reduce desertification?
p1: Solar cookers use free solar energy so women need not collect firewood → less deforestation; they are cheap and simple, but food cooks slowly and must be left outside.
p2: Crop rotation → farmers are taught about nutrients and soil exhaustion; legumes such as peas and beans are nitrogen fixers that boost soil fertility.
p3: Crop rotation is cheap but relies on a robust education system or NGOs; skills can be passed to other villages and to the farmers' children.
s: Solar cookers use free solar energy so women need not collect firewood → less deforestation; they are cheap and simple, but food cooks slowly and must be left outside.
Crop rotation → farmers are taught about nutrients and soil exhaustion; legumes such as peas and beans are nitrogen fixers that boost soil fertility.
Crop rotation is cheap but relies on a robust education system or NGOs; skills can be passed to other villages and to the farmers' children.

front: What is development?
p1: Development is progress in a country's quality of life and standard of living; the latter is money and material wealth, mostly measurable, e.g. GDP per capita, wages and electricity access.
p2: Quality of life is how good life feels and how satisfied people are, including health, safety, a clean environment and freedom; it is more subjective and harder to measure.
p3: The World Bank sorts countries by GNI per capita into low, lower-middle, upper-middle and high income; NEE is not a World Bank category but describes middle income countries developing quickly.
s: Development is progress in a country's quality of life and standard of living; the latter is money and material wealth, mostly measurable, e.g. GDP per capita, wages and electricity access.
Quality of life is how good life feels and how satisfied people are, including health, safety, a clean environment and freedom; it is more subjective and harder to measure.
The World Bank sorts countries by GNI per capita into low, lower-middle, upper-middle and high income; NEE is not a World Bank category but describes middle income countries developing quickly.

front: How is development measured?
p1: Economic indicators measure an economy, e.g. GNI per capita (Nigeria about $2,160, UK about $46,000+); social indicators measure wider quality of life; composite indicators combine several.
p2: The Human Development Index is a composite of life expectancy, education and GNI per capita, scored 0 to 1 → Nigeria about 0.54, UK about 0.93.
p3: Nigeria against the UK → infant mortality about 72 against 3.6 per 1,000; life expectancy about 53 to 55 against 81 years; literacy about 62% against 99%.
s: Economic indicators measure an economy, e.g. GNI per capita (Nigeria about $2,160, UK about $46,000+); social indicators measure wider quality of life; composite indicators combine several.
The Human Development Index is a composite of life expectancy, education and GNI per capita, scored 0 to 1 → Nigeria about 0.54, UK about 0.93.
Nigeria against the UK → infant mortality about 72 against 3.6 per 1,000; life expectancy about 53 to 55 against 81 years; literacy about 62% against 99%.

front: What is the demographic transition model?
p1: The demographic transition model shows how a population changes as a country develops; stage 1 has very high, fluctuating birth and death rates, so natural increase is very low.
p2: Stage 2 → death rate falls rapidly as healthcare, hygiene and living standards improve while birth rate stays high → population explosion; Nigeria's wide-based pyramid is a stage 2 shape.
p3: Stage 3 → birth rate falls rapidly as contraception becomes more available and more women work; stage 4 has low rates, with growth mainly from immigration; the UK is stage 4/5.
s: The demographic transition model shows how a population changes as a country develops; stage 1 has very high, fluctuating birth and death rates, so natural increase is very low.
Stage 2 → death rate falls rapidly as healthcare, hygiene and living standards improve while birth rate stays high → population explosion; Nigeria's wide-based pyramid is a stage 2 shape.
Stage 3 → birth rate falls rapidly as contraception becomes more available and more women work; stage 4 has low rates, with growth mainly from immigration; the UK is stage 4/5.

front: Where is Nigeria?
p1: Nigeria is in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea, bordering Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon; it covers about 924,000 km², nearly four times the size of the UK.
p2: Abuja was purpose-built in the centre and became capital in 1991 → seen as neutral ground between the main ethnic groups; it replaced Lagos, still the biggest city.
p3: About 218 million people → the most populous country in Africa; more than 250 ethnic groups speak around 500 languages, with English official; Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are the largest.
s: Nigeria is in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea, bordering Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon; it covers about 924,000 km², nearly four times the size of the UK.
Abuja was purpose-built in the centre and became capital in 1991 → seen as neutral ground between the main ethnic groups; it replaced Lagos, still the biggest city.
About 218 million people → the most populous country in Africa; more than 250 ethnic groups speak around 500 languages, with English official; Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are the largest.

front: Why is Nigeria important?
p1: Culture: Nollywood is the second largest film industry in the world, Afrobeats has global audiences, and Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986.
p2: Economy: once seen as Africa's largest, now third on the IMF's 2026 outlook; 70% work in agriculture; supplies 2.7% of the world's oil, the 12th largest producer.
p3: International: member of OPEC since 1971, founding member of ECOWAS in 1975, and the 5th largest contributor to UN peacekeeping.
s: Culture: Nollywood is the second largest film industry in the world, Afrobeats has global audiences, and Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986.
Economy: once seen as Africa's largest, now third on the IMF's 2026 outlook; 70% work in agriculture; supplies 2.7% of the world's oil, the 12th largest producer.
International: member of OPEC since 1971, founding member of ECOWAS in 1975, and the 5th largest contributor to UN peacekeeping.

front: How did history shape Nigeria's development?
p1: Britain ruled Nigeria from the mid-19th century until independence in 1960 → palm oil, peanuts and cocoa were extracted as raw materials, with no factories or education developed.
p2: It became a gate keeper state → the only way to gain wealth and power was to control the 'gate', such as the port; borders drawn by Europeans ignored ethnic, religious and cultural differences.
p3: Civil war lasted from 1967 to 1970, then dictatorships followed, with no stable democracy until 1999; the north suffers drought and desertification.
s: Britain ruled Nigeria from the mid-19th century until independence in 1960 → palm oil, peanuts and cocoa were extracted as raw materials, with no factories or education developed.
It became a gate keeper state → the only way to gain wealth and power was to control the 'gate', such as the port; borders drawn by Europeans ignored ethnic, religious and cultural differences.
Civil war lasted from 1967 to 1970, then dictatorships followed, with no stable democracy until 1999; the north suffers drought and desertification.

front: How does the development gap lead to migration?
p1: The gap in standard of living and wealth between richer and poorer countries drives migration; push factors include low wages or conflict, pull factors include jobs.
p2: In Kano and Sokoto over 70% live on under $1.90 a day; maternal mortality is about 917 per 100,000 against 512 nationally; the north has 0.24 doctors per 1,000, the south 1.3.
p3: About 10 million move to cities like Lagos each year; 1.3 million Nigerians have migrated abroad; remittances of about $23 billion in 2021 help families but can deepen inequality.
s: The gap in standard of living and wealth between richer and poorer countries drives migration; push factors include low wages or conflict, pull factors include jobs.
In Kano and Sokoto over 70% live on under $1.90 a day; maternal mortality is about 917 per 100,000 against 512 nationally; the north has 0.24 doctors per 1,000, the south 1.3.
About 10 million move to cities like Lagos each year; 1.3 million Nigerians have migrated abroad; remittances of about $23 billion in 2021 help families but can deepen inequality.

front: How can manufacturing and tourism help Nigeria?
p1: Nigeria's employment is about 34% primary, 18% secondary and 48% tertiary; the Clark-Fisher model shows how jobs change in a predictable order as a country develops.
p2: Tourism contributed about 4.5% of GDP in 2019 and employs 2.4 million; Lagos is the largest centre, with the Lekki beaches, and Badagry is linked to the Atlantic slave trade.
p3: Positive multiplier effect → spending creates jobs → more money in the local economy → better roads, airports and power; costs include economic leakage, seasonal low-paid jobs and litter.
s: Nigeria's employment is about 34% primary, 18% secondary and 48% tertiary; the Clark-Fisher model shows how jobs change in a predictable order as a country develops.
Tourism contributed about 4.5% of GDP in 2019 and employs 2.4 million; Lagos is the largest centre, with the Lekki beaches, and Badagry is linked to the Atlantic slave trade.
Positive multiplier effect → spending creates jobs → more money in the local economy → better roads, airports and power; costs include economic leakage, seasonal low-paid jobs and litter.

front: How else can aid and trade close the development gap?
p1: Official Development Assistance (ODA) passes from one government to another on a large scale; aid direct between governments is bilateral, aid through the World Bank is multilateral.
p2: Nigeria gets about 4% of Africa's aid; the World Bank gave $495 million for water management, including the Farin Ruwa dam; this aid is a loan, repaid with interest → debt.
p3: Problems → about $40 million is lost to corruption each year; up to 90% of ODA can be a loan; about $30 billion flows into Africa yearly but more flows out.
s: Official Development Assistance (ODA) passes from one government to another on a large scale; aid direct between governments is bilateral, aid through the World Bank is multilateral.
Nigeria gets about 4% of Africa's aid; the World Bank gave $495 million for water management, including the Farin Ruwa dam; this aid is a loan, repaid with interest → debt.
Problems → about $40 million is lost to corruption each year; up to 90% of ODA can be a loan; about $30 billion flows into Africa yearly but more flows out.

front: What other strategies can close the development gap?
p1: Simple, low-cost technology that suits local skills, e.g. hand pumps, is intermediate technology; it is cheap and locally controlled but small scale.
p2: Farmers get a fair, guaranteed price plus money for their community and better working conditions under Fairtrade; products cost more.
p3: Debt relief cancels or reduces money owed, freeing money for health and education, but often has conditions; microfinance gives very small loans to people refused by banks, empowering women, but interest can be high.
s: Simple, low-cost technology that suits local skills, e.g. hand pumps, is intermediate technology; it is cheap and locally controlled but small scale.
Farmers get a fair, guaranteed price plus money for their community and better working conditions under Fairtrade; products cost more.

Debt relief cancels or reduces money owed, freeing money for health and education, but often has conditions; microfinance gives very small loans to people refused by banks, empowering women, but interest can be high.

front: How do TNCs affect Nigeria?
p1: The Niger Delta is the centre of Nigeria's oil industry → about 50 oil fields and 5,000 km of pipelines; oil gives about 90% of export income; Shell, Exxon, Chevron and Eni operate there.
p2: Positives → Shell employs over 4,500 directly and 20,000 indirectly, creating a multiplier effect; TNCs pay tax for schools and roads and bring new technology.
p3: Negatives → economic leakage as profits return to HICs; insecure jobs; about 240,000 barrels spilt a year, up to 25 years to clean.
s: The Niger Delta is the centre of Nigeria's oil industry → about 50 oil fields and 5,000 km of pipelines; oil gives about 90% of export income; Shell, Exxon, Chevron and Eni operate there.
Positives → Shell employs over 4,500 directly and 20,000 indirectly, creating a multiplier effect; TNCs pay tax for schools and roads and bring new technology.
Negatives → economic leakage as profits return to HICs; insecure jobs; about 240,000 barrels spilt a year, up to 25 years to clean.

front: What is the evidence for climate change?
p1: Short term → temperatures up about 1°C since the late 19th century; ice sheets shrinking, glaciers retreating; sea level up 20 cm in a century, the rate nearly double in the last two decades.
p2: Long term → ice cores from Antarctica and Greenland reach 3 km deep; the oldest go back 800,000 years (Antarctica); trapped air bubbles show past carbon dioxide and methane.
p3: Ocean-floor sediment cores hold microorganisms that record past ocean temperature; direct carbon dioxide measurements go back only to the 1950s.
s: Short term → temperatures up about 1°C since the late 19th century; ice sheets shrinking, glaciers retreating; sea level up 20 cm in a century, the rate nearly double in the last two decades.
Long term → ice cores from Antarctica and Greenland reach 3 km deep; the oldest go back 800,000 years (Antarctica); trapped air bubbles show past carbon dioxide and methane.
Ocean-floor sediment cores hold microorganisms that record past ocean temperature; direct carbon dioxide measurements go back only to the 1950s.

front: What causes climate change?
p1: Natural factors → orbital changes, volcanic activity and solar output; the natural greenhouse effect helps sustain life on Earth.
p2: Human factors → burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas → more heat trapped, the enhanced greenhouse effect.
p3: Livestock farming produces methane, which traps heat more effectively than carbon dioxide; deforestation removes carbon sinks, forests that absorb more carbon than they release.
s: Natural factors → orbital changes, volcanic activity and solar output; the natural greenhouse effect helps sustain life on Earth.
Human factors → burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas → more heat trapped, the enhanced greenhouse effect.
Livestock farming produces methane, which traps heat more effectively than carbon dioxide; deforestation removes carbon sinks, forests that absorb more carbon than they release.

front: Who is responsible for climate change?
p1: Just 100 companies are the source of more than 70% of greenhouse gas emissions since 1988 → 25 of them account for more than half of global industrial emissions.
p2: ExxonMobil, Shell, BP and Chevron are among the highest emitting investor-owned companies; extraction at the 1988 to 2017 rate → temperatures on course to rise 4°C by 2100.
p3: A carbon sink is a natural environment such as oceans or forests that absorbs more carbon than it releases, so lowering carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
s: Just 100 companies are the source of more than 70% of greenhouse gas emissions since 1988 → 25 of them account for more than half of global industrial emissions.
ExxonMobil, Shell, BP and Chevron are among the highest emitting investor-owned companies; extraction at the 1988 to 2017 rate → temperatures on course to rise 4°C by 2100.
A carbon sink is a natural environment such as oceans or forests that absorbs more carbon than it releases, so lowering carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

front: What are the effects of climate change?
p1: Temperatures are about 1.2°C above pre-industrial levels → glaciers and ice caps melt and sea levels rise → flooding of low-lying places such as the Maldives and parts of Bangladesh.
p2: Rainfall changes → crop failures and food shortages in parts of Africa and South Asia; Himalayan glacial melt threatens water for millions on the Ganges; droughts in California.
p3: Polar bears lose sea ice; coral bleaching hits the Great Barrier Reef as coral expels algae; Amazon wildfires release stored carbon → a feedback loop.
s: Temperatures are about 1.2°C above pre-industrial levels → glaciers and ice caps melt and sea levels rise → flooding of low-lying places such as the Maldives and parts of Bangladesh.
Rainfall changes → crop failures and food shortages in parts of Africa and South Asia; Himalayan glacial melt threatens water for millions on the Ganges; droughts in California.
Polar bears lose sea ice; coral bleaching hits the Great Barrier Reef as coral expels algae; Amazon wildfires release stored carbon → a feedback loop.

front: How can we mitigate climate change?
p1: Mitigation reduces greenhouse gas emissions → alternative energy such as solar, wind and hydroelectric cuts fossil fuel use; trees absorb carbon dioxide as natural carbon sinks, but non-native species can disrupt ecosystems.
p2: CCS captures carbon dioxide from industry and stores it underground; it is still being developed and costly but could cut emissions from cement and steel.
p3: The Paris Agreement, adopted by nearly every country, aims to keep warming well below 2°C and to aim for 1.5°C; the challenge is that nations follow through on their commitments.
s: Mitigation reduces greenhouse gas emissions → alternative energy such as solar, wind and hydroelectric cuts fossil fuel use; trees absorb carbon dioxide as natural carbon sinks, but non-native species can disrupt ecosystems.
CCS captures carbon dioxide from industry and stores it underground; it is still being developed and costly but could cut emissions from cement and steel.
The Paris Agreement, adopted by nearly every country, aims to keep warming well below 2°C and to aim for 1.5°C; the challenge is that nations follow through on their commitments.

front: How can we adapt to climate change?
p1: Adaptation means changing how we live to suit the new environment; in farming this means changing to more resilient crop varieties and adjusting planting schedules.
p2: Managing water supply → rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation and sustainable groundwater management help communities use water efficiently in droughts.
p3: Reducing risk from rising sea levels → sea walls and flood barriers, plus restoring wetlands that absorb excess water.
s: Adaptation means changing how we live to suit the new environment; in farming this means changing to more resilient crop varieties and adjusting planting schedules.
Managing water supply → rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation and sustainable groundwater management help communities use water efficiently in droughts.
Reducing risk from rising sea levels → sea walls and flood barriers, plus restoring wetlands that absorb excess water.

front: How does a river erode and transport?
p1: Water forced into cracks in the bank weakens the rock until it breaks away, which is hydraulic action; rocks carried by the river rub against the bed and bank, wearing them away, which is abrasion.
p2: Rocks carried by the river smash together and break into smaller, smoother, rounder pebbles, which is attrition.
p3: Solution dissolves minerals; suspension carries fine silt; saltation bounces pebbles along the bed; traction rolls boulders as bedload; material is deposited when the water loses energy.
s: Water forced into cracks in the bank weakens the rock until it breaks away, which is hydraulic action; rocks carried by the river rub against the bed and bank, wearing them away, which is abrasion.
Rocks carried by the river smash together and break into smaller, smoother, rounder pebbles, which is attrition.
Solution dissolves minerals; suspension carries fine silt; saltation bounces pebbles along the bed; traction rolls boulders as bedload; material is deposited when the water loses energy.

front: How do upper course landforms form?
p1: Upland streams have low discharge → up to 95% of energy overcomes friction and the rest erodes vertically; steep, unsupported sides are attacked by freeze-thaw weathering → a V-shaped valley.
p2: The river winds around more resistant rock and cuts into weaker rock, leaving interlocking spurs.
p3: A waterfall forms by differential erosion → hard rock over soft; in the plunge pool hydraulic action and abrasion undercut the soft rock, the overhang collapses and a gorge forms as the waterfall retreats.
s: Upland streams have low discharge → up to 95% of energy overcomes friction and the rest erodes vertically; steep, unsupported sides are attacked by freeze-thaw weathering → a V-shaped valley.
The river winds around more resistant rock and cuts into weaker rock, leaving interlocking spurs.

A waterfall forms by differential erosion → hard rock over soft; in the plunge pool hydraulic action and abrasion undercut the soft rock, the overhang collapses and a gorge forms as the waterfall retreats.

front: How do middle and lower course landforms form?
p1: At a meander the outside bank is undercut by lateral erosion where the current is faster, forming a river cliff; sand and shingle are deposited on the slower inside bend.
p2: In low flow, bed load is deposited and raises the river bed, increasing flood risk; in a flood the heaviest sediment drops closest to the river.
p3: Raised banks formed by repeated flooding are natural levees; the floodplain is low-lying ground next to a river, formed mainly of river sediments and subject to flooding.
s: At a meander the outside bank is undercut by lateral erosion where the current is faster, forming a river cliff; sand and shingle are deposited on the slower inside bend.
In low flow, bed load is deposited and raises the river bed, increasing flood risk; in a flood the heaviest sediment drops closest to the river.
Raised banks formed by repeated flooding are natural levees; the floodplain is low-lying ground next to a river, formed mainly of river sediments and subject to flooding.

front: What causes river flooding?
p1: A flood is when river level rises until it overflows its banks; physical causes include rainfall, geology, relief and vegetation.
p2: Impermeable rock stops water soaking in → it reaches the river by surface runoff, the quickest route → shorter lag time → river more likely to overflow.
p3: Human causes → urbanisation, building on floodplains, deforestation and arable farming; concrete and tarmac are impermeable, so rain runs rapidly into drains and rivers.
s: A flood is when river level rises until it overflows its banks; physical causes include rainfall, geology, relief and vegetation.
Impermeable rock stops water soaking in → it reaches the river by surface runoff, the quickest route → shorter lag time → river more likely to overflow.
Human causes → urbanisation, building on floodplains, deforestation and arable farming; concrete and tarmac are impermeable, so rain runs rapidly into drains and rivers.

front: How was Boscastle flooded and managed?
p1: On 16 August 2004 heavy localised rain, 89mm in an hour, fell on saturated ground; a steep-sided impermeable valley funnelled water into the village and narrow river channels.
p2: Hard engineering uses man-made structures to prevent or control natural processes; soft engineering works with natural processes to manage flood risk.
p3: The Boscastle scheme cost £4.5 million and took four years → it reduced appeal in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, cutting tourism; unstable trees were removed, destroying habitats.
s: On 16 August 2004 heavy localised rain, 89mm in an hour, fell on saturated ground; a steep-sided impermeable valley funnelled water into the village and narrow river channels.
Hard engineering uses man-made structures to prevent or control natural processes; soft engineering works with natural processes to manage flood risk.
The Boscastle scheme cost £4.5 million and took four years → it reduced appeal in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, cutting tourism; unstable trees were removed, destroying habitats.

front: What are the types of wave?
p1: Low waves with a strong swash push sand and pebbles up the beach and build it up; these are constructive waves.
p2: High waves with a strong backwash drag material back into the sea and erode beaches and cliffs; these are destructive waves.
p3: Weathering is when rocks are broken up in situ, not removed; erosion removes material; both shape coastal landscapes.
s: Low waves with a strong swash push sand and pebbles up the beach and build it up; these are constructive waves.
High waves with a strong backwash drag material back into the sea and erode beaches and cliffs; these are destructive waves.
Weathering is when rocks are broken up in situ, not removed; erosion removes material; both shape coastal landscapes.

front: How do headlands and bays form?
p1: Bands of alternating rock running parallel to the coast form a concordant coastline; bands at right angles to the coast form a discordant coastline.
p2: Swanage on the Jurassic Coast is a discordant coastline, so headlands and bays form there; less resistant rock erodes more rapidly than resistant rock.
p3: A headland is a cliff that juts out into the sea, surrounded by water on three sides; a bay is a crescent-shaped indentation in the coastline.
s: Bands of alternating rock running parallel to the coast form a concordant coastline; bands at right angles to the coast form a discordant coastline.
Swanage on the Jurassic Coast is a discordant coastline, so headlands and bays form there; less resistant rock erodes more rapidly than resistant rock.
A headland is a cliff that juts out into the sea, surrounded by water on three sides; a bay is a crescent-shaped indentation in the coastline.

front: How do cliffs and stacks form?
p1: A wave cut notch forms at the cliff base between high and low water mark, cut by hydraulic action; the cliff above is undercut and collapses, leaving a wave cut platform.
p2: Waves erode a crack into a cave, then an arch; when the arch collapses a stack is left, which is eroded down to a low stump.
p3: Vegetation on a cliff shows biological weathering is taking place: plant roots exert force and release weak acids that break up the rock.
s: A wave cut notch forms at the cliff base between high and low water mark, cut by hydraulic action; the cliff above is undercut and collapses, leaving a wave cut platform.
Waves erode a crack into a cave, then an arch; when the arch collapses a stack is left, which is eroded down to a low stump.
Vegetation on a cliff shows biological weathering is taking place: plant roots exert force and release weak acids that break up the rock.

front: How are depositional landforms formed?
p1: Longshore drift moves material along the coast in a zigzag → the prevailing wind drives waves in at an angle; swash carries material up the beach, backwash returns it by gravity.
p2: Landforms of deposition such as spits form where material moved by longshore drift is dropped; a bar is a spit that cuts off a bay.
p3: Sand blown inland is stabilised by plants such as marram grass → embryo dunes by the sea, then yellow dunes, then older grey dunes; a slack is the dip between dunes.
s: Longshore drift moves material along the coast in a zigzag → the prevailing wind drives waves in at an angle; swash carries material up the beach, backwash returns it by gravity.
Landforms of deposition such as spits form where material moved by longshore drift is dropped; a bar is a spit that cuts off a bay.
Sand blown inland is stabilised by plants such as marram grass → embryo dunes by the sea, then yellow dunes, then older grey dunes; a slack is the dip between dunes.

front: How can coasts be managed?
p1: Hard engineering uses large artificial structures to stop erosion or flooding; soft engineering is less intrusive and works with natural processes; the Holderness Coast loses about 2 metres a year.
p2: Managed retreat, also called managed realignment, removes coastal protection so low-lying land is deliberately flooded; costs are low and salt marsh protects against storms, but land and property are lost.
p3: Groynes stop longshore drift and keep the beach in place; hard defences can cause conflict further along the coast where sediment supply is interrupted.
s: Hard engineering uses large artificial structures to stop erosion or flooding; soft engineering is less intrusive and works with natural processes; the Holderness Coast loses about 2 metres a year.

Managed retreat, also called managed realignment, removes coastal protection so low-lying land is deliberately flooded; costs are low and salt marsh protects against storms, but land and property are lost.
Groynes stop longshore drift and keep the beach in place; hard defences can cause conflict further along the coast where sediment supply is interrupted.

front: Why does Walton on the Naze need managing?
p1: Walton on the Naze is the Paper 1 case study and Paper 3 fieldwork site; permeable red crag over impermeable London clay slumps, and destructive waves attack the soft cliffs.
p2: The Essex coast loses about 2 m a year, historically up to 16 m; the Naze Tower was 400 m from the coast and is now just a few metres away.
p3: The cliffs are an SSSI rich in fossils up to 55 million years old; erosion also threatens properties such as Sunny Point road, where the average house costs £400,000.

front: How is Walton on the Naze managed?
p1: In 1977 a seawall, breakwaters and groynes protected properties in the south; groynes stop longshore drift, but many are now old, rotten and buried by sand.
p2: In the north the replenished beach was mostly gone by 2003; the cliff was then regraded and planted, a soft strategy that binds the soil.

front: What conditions do tropical storms need?
p1: Sea surface temperature above 27°C to a depth of at least 60 m → intense evaporation saturates the air with water vapour.
p2: Trade winds converge near the Equator and force warm, moist air to rise → pressure falls; the rising air cools and condenses into cumulonimbus clouds.
p3: The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation, deflects incoming air and starts the spiral; storms do not form within about 5° of the Equator because the force is too weak.

Trade winds converge near the Equator and force warm, moist air to rise → pressure falls; the rising air cools and condenses into cumulonimbus clouds.
The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation, deflects incoming air and starts the spiral; storms do not form within about 5° of the Equator because the force is too weak.

front: How does a tropical storm develop and die?
p1: A tropical disturbance strengthens into a tropical depression, then a tropical storm, and eventually a tropical cyclone, hurricane or typhoon.
p2: At the centre is a calm eye of descending air; around it the eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain; spiral rainbands draw in warm, moist air.
p3: Warm ocean water is the energy source; at landfall or over cooler water the energy supply is cut off → friction and loss of warm moisture weaken the storm.

front: What happened in Typhoon Haiyan?
p1: Haiyan struck the Philippines on 8 November 2013 as a category 5 storm; a storm surge and about 400 mm of rain flooded up to 1 km inland, destroying about 90% of Tacloban.
p2: Primary effects → power cut, airport damaged, roads blocked; three-quarters of farmers and fishers lost income; oil from a barge contaminated 10 hectares of mangrove.
p3: Secondary effects → contaminated water raised waterborne disease; shortages caused looting and eight deaths in a stampede for rice; rice prices rose 11.9% by 2014.

front: How did people respond to Typhoon Haiyan?
p1: About 800,000 people were evacuated to stadiums in Tacloban, but some flooded; the Red Cross gave out rice and canned food; airport damage delayed aid by up to three days.
p2: France, Belgium and Israel set up field hospitals; the USA used the carrier USS George Washington's helicopters for search and rescue and supplies.
p3: Cash-for-work paid locals to clear debris; agencies replaced fishing boats; cyclone shelters and surge warnings were built; a no-build zone was often ineffective as people fish from the coast.

front: How can the effects of tropical storms be reduced?
p1: Prediction → satellite data let the US National Hurricane Centre predict Katrina's landfall 56 hours before it hit New Orleans; some countries lack accurate modelling data.
p2: Preparation → emergency shelters on higher ground away from storm surges; information is broadcast on TV, radio and social media, or by loudspeakers in some developing countries.
p3: Protection → key roads may be elevated in surge-prone areas, but it is hard to protect everywhere; low-lying, poor areas without defences are most at risk.

front: Why do people live in hazard zones?
p1: Living with danger is a way of life; family and friends give roots in a place; some people study hazards, e.g. vulcanologists and storm chasers.
p2: Money can be made from tourism or farming; resources such as metals, minerals and precious stones are often found near volcanoes.
p3: Some hazard areas are huge settlements, e.g. Mexico City in an earthquake zone, which cannot be moved; the bottom line is often poverty, with little choice about where to live.

front: What extreme weather affects the UK?
p1: Storms begin as depressions, areas of low pressure, carried by the jet stream; Storm Darragh in December 2024 brought winds of about 96 mph in Devon and a rare red wind warning.
p2: Storm Babet in October 2023 brought 150 to 200 mm of rain to eastern Scotland; the River South Esk overwhelmed defences at Brechin and seven people died.
p3: Management is mostly preparation → the Met Office issues warnings and trees near power lines are maintained; flood walls, tree planting and floodplain planning reduce flood risk.

front: How do UK heat and cold extremes compare?
p1: Heatwaves often occur when an anticyclone sits over Britain → sinking air, clear skies; on 19 July 2022 Coningsby in Lincolnshire reached 40.3°C, the UK record.
p2: Droughts shrink rivers and reservoirs; water companies bring in hosepipe bans; days above 25°C rose 53% when 1991 to 2020 is compared with the previous 30 years.
p3: A change of wind direction can bring Arctic or polar continental air; over 17,000 trains were cancelled in January 2014; cold spells are expected to decrease as Britain warms.
